query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Ductility in metals can be enhanced by alloying with elements that promote face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal structures.
generation.material_initial_state: Pure metals with body-centered cubic (BCC) structures, such as iron.
generation.intervention: Alloying with elements like nickel or aluminum to promote FCC structures.
generation.conditions: Controlled temperature and pressure during alloying to ensure uniform distribution of alloying elements.
generation.structural_mediator: Crystal structure transformation from BCC to FCC.
generation.mechanism: The FCC structure allows for more slip systems, which enhances the ability of the material to deform plastically under stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ductility of the alloy will increase compared to the pure BCC metal.
generation.baseline: Ductility of pure iron (BCC) is relatively low compared to FCC metals.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies specifically to metals and does not extend to non-metallic materials.
generation.uncertainty: The exact increase in ductility will depend on the specific alloying elements and their concentrations.

falsification_experiment.design: Create a series of alloys with varying concentrations of nickel and aluminum and test their ductility using tensile tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ductility of the alloys does not exceed that of pure iron, the hypothesis is falsified.
